## What will we learn?

Can clinical measurements help us distinguish patients with and without heart
disease? We will first read the results of a random forest already fitted to
these data. Then we will build a neural network and examine its predictions.

By the end, you should be able to explain a model's mistakes, fit a neural
network with Keras, and use `mlr3` to evaluate its predictions.

Have the [session guide](guide.qmd) ready before starting. It covers opening the
project and installing Keras. The code below assumes your working folder is
`part2/`. Run the code blocks in order in RStudio during the session. Saved results let
us discuss the examples before fitting our own network.

## 1. Meet the heart data

Each row describes one patient. There are 270 patients and 13 measurements,
including age, chest pain and cholesterol. The outcome, `heart_disease`, tells
us whether heart disease is `absent` or `present`. We are classifying existing
heart disease, rather than estimating future risk.

Load the prepared data. The data script gives the categories readable labels.

```{r}
#| label: neural-data
# Load the patient measurements and outcome labels.
source("R/01-data.R")
```

Count the patients in each outcome group:

```{r}
table(heart$heart_disease)
```

There are 150 patients without heart disease and 120 with heart disease.
A **predictor** is a measurement we use to help predict the outcome. The outcome
itself must not be included among the predictors.

**Discuss:** Which measurements might help distinguish the two groups?

## 2. Read the random forest results

A random forest combines predictions from many decision trees. We have already
fitted this model using 180 patients and tested it on the other 90. The test
patients were kept out of training so we could assess predictions on unseen
observations. We will use the saved results here, without fitting the forest
again.

### What did the model get right and wrong?

A **confusion matrix** counts correct predictions and mistakes. Read the rows
as the model's predictions and the columns as the patients' recorded outcomes.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Read the saved confusion matrix"
forest_confusion <- read.csv("outputs/confusion.csv")
forest_table <- xtabs(Freq ~ response + truth, data = forest_confusion)
knitr::kable(forest_table, caption = "Random forest: predictions for 90 test patients")
```

The model correctly identified 30 patients with heart disease and 45 without it.
It missed 7 patients who had heart disease (**false negatives**) and raised
8 false alarms in patients without heart disease (**false positives**).

**Discuss:** What might a missed case mean for a patient? What might a false
alarm lead to?

### How well did it perform?

**Accuracy** is the proportion of all test patients classified correctly.
**Sensitivity** is the proportion of patients with heart disease correctly
identified. **Specificity** is the proportion without heart disease correctly
identified.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Read the saved forest scores"
forest_scores <- read.csv("outputs/holdout-measures.csv")
measure_ids <- c("classif.acc", "classif.tpr", "classif.tnr")
measure_labels <- c("Accuracy", "Sensitivity", "Specificity")
forest_values <- forest_scores$value[match(measure_ids, forest_scores$measure)]

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(Measure = measure_labels, Percent = round(100 * forest_values, 1)),
  caption = "Saved random forest results (%)"
)
```

Accuracy is 83.3%: 75 correct predictions out of 90. Sensitivity is 81.1% and
specificity is 84.9%. Looking at all three helps us see what accuracy alone
can hide.

The forest predicts probabilities. A **threshold** is the probability at which
we decide to classify a patient as having heart disease. Lowering the threshold
usually catches more cases, but also raises more false alarms.

![The ROC curve shows sensitivity against the false-positive rate as the probability threshold changes. The diagonal represents chance-level discrimination.](figures/04-roc.png){fig-align="center"}

**Discuss:** Would you choose a threshold using accuracy alone?

## 3. Use mlr3 to organise the prediction task

We now ask the same question using a neural network. We keep the same training
and test patients so the results can be compared.

`mlr3` helps organise a prediction problem. A **task** records the data and the
outcome we want to predict. Here, `present` is the **positive class**: the
condition we want to detect. We load the saved split instead of drawing a new
one.

```{r}
#| label: neural-task
library(mlr3)
# Tell mlr3 which outcome to predict and which class means disease is present.
heart_task <- as_task_classif(heart,
  target = "heart_disease",
  positive = "present",
  id = "heart"
)
# Reuse the patients used to train and test the saved random forest.
split_record <- read.csv("outputs/split.csv")
split <- list(
  train = split_record$row_id[split_record$subset == "train"],
  test = split_record$row_id[split_record$subset == "test"]
)
```

The training group contains 180 patients; the test group contains 90. Keep the
test patients aside until the network has finished learning.

## 4. Prepare the inputs

Keras needs numerical inputs. We turn categories into numbers and indicator
columns. An **indicator** is a column containing 0 or 1 to show whether a category
applies. This gives us 22 input columns from the original 13 predictors.

We also **scale** numerical measurements so differences in units, such as age
and cholesterol, do not dominate the learning process. Scaling is learned from
the fitting rows only, keeping validation and test patients out of that step.

```{r}
#| label: neural-inputs
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show input preparation"
# Exclude the outcome from the inputs. Keras needs numbers, so use 0/1 for
# binary categories and indicator columns for the others. An indicator is 1
# when a category applies and 0 otherwise. Together these give 22 inputs.
x_data <- heart[, setdiff(names(heart), "heart_disease")]
for (nm in c("sex", "fasting_blood_sugar", "exercise_induced_angina")) {
  x_data[[nm]] <- as.integer(x_data[[nm]]) - 1L
}
nominal <- names(x_data)[vapply(x_data, is.factor, logical(1))]
contrasts_full <- lapply(x_data[nominal], function(x) contrasts(x, contrasts = FALSE))
x <- model.matrix(~ . - 1, data = x_data, contrasts.arg = contrasts_full)
stopifnot(ncol(x) == 22L, all(is.finite(x)))
# Keras reserves the last 20% of training rows for validation.
# Calculate scaling from the other 80% only, keeping validation and test
# patients out of this calculation.
inner_n <- floor(length(split$train) * 0.8)
fit_rows <- split$train[seq_len(inner_n)]
continuous <- names(x_data)[vapply(x_data, is.numeric, logical(1))]
continuous <- setdiff(
  continuous,
  c("sex", "fasting_blood_sugar", "exercise_induced_angina")
)
# Subtract each measurement's mean and divide by its standard deviation.
# This puts measurements with different units on a comparable scale.
centre <- colMeans(x[fit_rows, continuous, drop = FALSE])
spread <- apply(x[fit_rows, continuous, drop = FALSE], 2, sd)
stopifnot(all(spread > 0))
x[, continuous] <- sweep(
  sweep(x[, continuous, drop = FALSE], 2, centre),
  2, spread, "/"
)
# Code the outcome as 1 for present and 0 for absent.
y <- as.integer(heart$heart_disease == "present")
```

Check the number of input columns and the outcome coding:

```{r}
#| eval: false
ncol(x)
table(y)
```

The outcome is coded as 1 for heart disease and 0 for its absence.

## 5. Build the network with Keras

Keras defines and trains the neural network. We use it directly here, then bring
its predictions into `mlr3` for evaluation.

Think of the network as a sequence:

**Patient measurements → hidden layers → probability of heart disease**

A **hidden layer** combines inputs into patterns that the network learns.
The final layer returns one probability between 0 and 1. The two hidden layers
below contain 64 and 32 units. **Dropout** temporarily switches off some units
during training to help limit overfitting: learning the training examples too
closely to work well on new patients.

```{r}
#| label: neural-build
#| eval: false
library(keras3)
# Fix the random starting point for the network.
set_random_seed(20261023)

# Pass 22 inputs through two hidden layers to one output probability.
# Dropout temporarily switches off some units during training to limit overfitting.
network <- keras_model_sequential(input_shape = c(22)) |>
  layer_dense(units = 64, activation = "relu") |>
  layer_dropout(rate = 0.4) |>
  layer_dense(units = 32, activation = "relu") |>
  layer_dropout(rate = 0.4) |>
  layer_dense(units = 1, activation = "sigmoid")
# Choose how to update the weights and measure prediction error.
# Binary cross-entropy is a loss for a two-class outcome.
compile(network,
  optimizer = optimizer_adam(learning_rate = 0.002),
  loss = "binary_crossentropy", metrics = "accuracy"
)
```

`compile()` sets how the network learns. The **optimiser** updates its weights
(the values controlling its connections). The **loss** measures prediction error;
binary cross-entropy is used for this two-class outcome.

## 6. Fit the network and watch it learn

An **epoch** is one pass through the fitting data. A **batch** is a smaller group
processed before updating the weights.

We reserve 20% of the training group for **validation**: checking progress during
learning. The network updates its weights using 144 patients and monitors its
progress on 36 validation patients. These are separate from the 90 test patients.
Early stopping ends training if validation loss stops improving.

```{r}
#| label: neural-fit
#| eval: false
# An epoch is one pass through the fitting rows; batches contain 32 rows.
# Monitor validation loss and stop after 10 epochs without improvement,
# restoring the weights from the best validation epoch.
training <- fit(
  network,
  x[split$train, ],
  y[split$train],
  epochs = 50,
  batch_size = 32,
  validation_split = 0.2,
  verbose = 1,
  callbacks = list(callback_early_stopping(patience = 10, restore_best_weights = TRUE))
)
```

Plot the history from your own run:

```{r}
#| label: neural-history
#| eval: false
# Compare training and validation loss as learning progresses.
plot(training)
```

Look for training and validation loss in this plot. The figure below comes
from the saved workshop run; your run may produce a different curve.

![Saved neural-network run: training and validation loss across successive passes through the fitting data. Lower loss means smaller prediction error.](figures/05-neural-loss.png){fig-align="center"}

If training loss keeps falling while validation loss rises, the network may be
overfitting.

**Discuss:** Why do we need validation patients as well as training patients?

## 7. Evaluate the network and compare results

Use the trained network to predict probabilities for the 90 test patients.
For this example, classify a probability of 0.5 or more as `present`.

`PredictionClassif$new()` puts the Keras predictions into an `mlr3` prediction
object. It stores the observed outcomes, predicted classes and probabilities.
We can then request the same measures used for the forest.

```{r}
#| label: neural-predict
#| eval: false
# Predict unseen test patients. Use 0.5 as the cut-off for a present prediction.
prob <- as.numeric(predict(network, x[split$test, ], verbose = 0))
class <- ifelse(prob >= 0.5, "present", "absent")
accuracy <- mean(class == as.character(heart$heart_disease[split$test]))
accuracy

# Bring the Keras predictions into mlr3 for the same evaluation measures.
network_pred <- PredictionClassif$new(
  task = heart_task,
  row_ids = split$test,
  truth = heart_task$truth(rows = split$test),
  response = class,
  prob = cbind(present = prob, absent = 1 - prob)
)
network_pred$confusion
network_pred$score(msrs(c("classif.acc", "classif.tpr", "classif.tnr")))
```

### What happened in the saved run?

The next table uses the saved network predictions, rather than fitting a new
network when the page opens.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Compare the saved results"
saved_network <- read.csv("outputs/neural-predictions.csv")
stopifnot(
  identical(saved_network$row_id, split$test),
  identical(saved_network$truth, as.character(heart$heart_disease[split$test]))
)
saved_prediction <- PredictionClassif$new(
  task = heart_task,
  row_ids = saved_network$row_id,
  truth = heart_task$truth(rows = saved_network$row_id),
  response = saved_network$prediction,
  prob = cbind(
    present = saved_network$probability_present,
    absent = 1 - saved_network$probability_present
  )
)
network_values <- unname(saved_prediction$score(msrs(measure_ids)))
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Measure = measure_labels,
    `Random forest (%)` = round(100 * forest_values, 1),
    `Neural network (%)` = round(100 * network_values, 1),
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  caption = "Saved results for the same 90 test patients"
)
```

The saved network classified 77 of the 90 test patients correctly, compared
with 75 for the forest. That small difference in one split does not establish
that neural networks are generally better. Compare the types of mistakes as
well as the overall accuracy. After your own run, use `network_pred` above to
inspect your results; this saved comparison table remains a reference.

**Discuss:** Which model missed fewer cases? Is the difference large enough to
change your conclusion?
